newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Serbs must stay, vote-Western envoys.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Serbs must stay, vote-Western envoys.

text.p: Western diplomats on Friday urged Serbs from Croatia's Eastern Slavonia enclave to accept the area's return to Zagreb rule as inevitable and to vote in the first post-war elections next month.

Britain's ambassador to Croatia, Gavin Hewitt, and 12 other ambassadors visited Eastern Slavonia on Thursday for talks with local Serb leaders and officials of the 5,000-strong U.N. mission (UNTAES), which monitors the enclave until July 15.

"Serb leaders have to persuade the people (in the enclave) to stay, take Croatian documents and to vote, excercising their civic and political rights as citizens of Croatia," Hewitt told a news conference in Zagreb.
"They must take full advantage of what is on offer," the diplomat added, referring to a human and minority rights package Zagreb has offered to the Serbs.

The U.N. Security Council endorsed the package and gave Zagreb the green light to go ahead with voting for local administrative bodies. The poll is scheduled for March 16, simultaneously with local elections elsewhere in Croatia.
Eastern Slavonia broke away from Croatia in 1991, opposing its secession from federal Yugoslavia. Zagreb wants full control of the enclave after the UNTAES mandate expires on July 15.
Croatia said it moved a step closer to reintegrating the enclave when local Serb officials agreed to the gradual implementation of Croatian laws, coming into effect in late February.

"We handed (a visiting Serb delegation) a large legal package relating to criminal and civil law, judiciary organisation and other Croatian regulations," Justice Minister Miroslav Separovic told state television on Friday.
The private Croatia Banka said on Friday it was ready to open branches in the two largest towns of the Eastern Slavonia, Vukovar and Beli Manastir, the Croatian state news agency HINA reported.
The Serbs have dismissed Croatia's package, demanding that the area remains a single administrative unit with more autonomy and not be divided in two counties, as Zagreb would have it.
The Serb leadership, Hewitt said, was confusing its people by "prevaricating on the issue (of reintegration) for years". "They haven't got the leadership they deserve," he added.
"We told them procrastination is no way forward... There is no room, no time for further delay," the diplomat added.

The Croatian Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had issued citizenship papers necessary for voters to 57,000 people, or two thirds of the Eastern Slavonia population. The U.N. has put the number of current residents higher, at roughly 120,000.
Many of them are Serb refugees from other rebel enclaves Zagreb retook by force in in 1995.
Hewitt said some Serbs would probably leave the area before elections. "It's an inevitable consequence of the uncertainty their leadership has created by wrong political actions".

"Any person leaving Croatia at this time must be making the wrong economic decision... The area needs huge financial resources for economic restructuring...It deserves it, but as part of Croatia and not a particular separate area," he said.
